title: standalone.sh is stale — generated from older core.sh, timestamp() differs
description:
standalone.sh line 362 has: function timestamp() { date +'%Y%m%d_%H%M%S'; }
core.sh line 361 has the Bash 4.2+ optimized version:
  if [[ "${BASH_VERSINFO[0]}" -gt 4 || ( "${BASH_VERSINFO[0]}" -eq 4 && "${BASH_VERSINFO[1]}" -ge 2 ) ]]; then
      printf '%(%Y%m%d_%H%M%S)T\n' -1
  else
      date +'%Y%m%d_%H%M%S'
  fi

The entire core section of standalone.sh (487 lines) differs from core.sh. This means standalone.sh was generated from an older version and must be regenerated with ./build.sh.

Impact: Users deploying standalone.sh get a less performant timestamp() and potentially other behavioral differences from core.sh.

title: wait_for_url() ((c++)) terminates script under set -e when c=0
description:
In core.sh line ~359:
  function wait_for_url() { local u="${1}" t="${2:-30}" c=0; until quiet curl -s --head --request GET "$u"; do sleep 1; ((c++)); [[ "$c" -ge "$t" ]] && return 1; done; return 0; }

When c=0, ((c++)) evaluates to 0 (post-increment returns the original value), which Bash treats as exit code 1. With set -e enabled (via safe_mode), this terminates the script on the very first iteration of the loop.

Fix: Use ((++c)) (pre-increment) or c=$((c + 1)) instead.

title: retry() loses argument boundaries via local -r cmd="$@"
description:
In core.sh line ~168:
  function retry() {
      local -r -i max_attempts="$1"; shift; local -r cmd="$@"; local -i attempt=1
      until eval "$cmd"; do

After shift, "$@" captures remaining arguments. But local -r cmd="$@" joins them with spaces into a single string. Then eval "$cmd" re-parses the string, which can break commands with:
- Arguments containing quotes (nested quoting issues)
- Arguments with backslashes (eval re-interprets them)
- Commands with complex quoting

Example: retry 3 my_command "arg with spaces" "another 'quoted' arg"
The quotes around 'another 'quoted' arg' may be lost or mangled.

Fix: Pass arguments individually and use a loop with the command array, or use a different retry mechanism that preserves argument boundaries.

title: timestamp() doc comment incorrectly claims optional argument
description:
In core.sh line ~355:
  # DESC: Format helpers
  # ARGS: $1 (optional): length or path
  # OUTS: Formatted string to stdout
  # RETS: 0
  function timestamp() { ... }

The function takes zero arguments. The doc comment incorrectly claims $1 (optional): length or path. This is documentation drift that misleads users.

title: Only 3 of 70+ functions tested — extensive untested public API
description:
tests/core.bats only tests 3 functions:
- is_sourced
- slugify
- is_int

core.sh has 70 functions total. The following critical functions have zero test coverage:
- safe_mode, check_dependencies, is_cmd, confirm, retry, is_empty
- is_int, is_alphanumeric, is_function, is_ssh, is_online, is_container
- check_bash_version, version_gt, timer_start, timer_stop
- abs_path, get_ext, random_string, to_lower, to_upper, trim, join_by, slugify
- indent, hr, box, run, quiet, spinner
- backup, mktemp_file, mktemp_dir, ensure_line
- get_json_val, wait_for_url
- lock, unlock
- pause, load_env, cron_init
- colour_init, debug_mode, log, info, warn, error, notice, out, append, overwrite, die

Test coverage is ~4%. Critical functions like retry(), lock(), load_env() and is_empty() have no tests.

title: lock() uses predictable filenames in /tmp — symlink attack vector
description:
In core.sh line ~385:
  function lock() {
      local scope="${1:-system}"
      local l
      if [[ "$scope" == "user" ]]; then
          l="/tmp/${__base}.${UID}.lock"
      else
          l="/tmp/${__base}.lock"
      fi
      if [[ -e "$l" ]]; then
          local p=$(cat "$l")
          kill -0 "$p" 2>/dev/null && die "Already running (PID: ${p})"
      fi
      echo "$$" > "$l"

The lock file path is predictable: /tmp/${script_name}.lock. An attacker can:
1. Create a symlink at /tmp/${script_name}.lock -> /etc/cron.d/malicious
2. The lock() call then overwrites the symlink target with the PID

Fix: Use mktemp for lock files, or use flock(1) for atomic locking.
